payload.text:
# Your workspace

You are in `/work`, inside a Linux container with no network access. Write a Go program here.
[Maelstrom](https://github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom) will start that program once for every node
of a simulated cluster, send it client requests, and check that the answers are correct.

What is installed:

- Go 1.27.
- Maelstrom 0.2.4, as the `maelstrom` command, so you can test your program yourself.
- Maelstrom's Go library, already in the module cache. Start your module with:

      go mod init node
      go get github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom/demo/go@v0.0.0-20260710121306-480a8197026d

A node talks to the rest of the cluster through standard input and output: it reads one JSON
message per line on stdin and writes one per line on stdout. Each message has a `src`, a `dest`
and a `body`, and the body's `type` says what it is. Anything written to stderr is a log line.
The library does that framing for you: `maelstrom.NewNode()`, then `Handle` a message type,
`Reply` to a request, `Send` or `RPC` to another node, and `Run` to start. It also answers the
`init` message that tells each node its own ID and the IDs of all the nodes.

# Broadcast on a single node

Write a node that keeps every value broadcast to it and reports them back when asked. Clients
send it three kinds of request.

`broadcast` gives the node a value to keep. The values are integers, and each one is sent once:

    {"type": "broadcast", "msg_id": 1, "message": 1000}
    {"type": "broadcast_ok", "in_reply_to": 1}

`read` asks for every value the node has, in any order:

    {"type": "read", "msg_id": 2}
    {"type": "read_ok", "in_reply_to": 2, "messages": [1000, 1001]}

`topology` tells the node which other nodes are its neighbours. It comes once, at the start:

    {"type": "topology", "msg_id": 3, "topology": {"n1": []}}
    {"type": "topology_ok", "in_reply_to": 3}

For now the cluster is a single node, so it has no neighbours, but the request must still be
answered. The answer to `read` must include every value whose `broadcast` was acknowledged.

## How it's graded

You have 30 minutes and 100 steps, a step being one reply from you, however many tools it runs. If either runs out, you are stopped where you are.

When you stop, your program is built with `go build -o node .` and tested 3 times with:

    maelstrom test --workload broadcast --bin ./node --node-count 1 --rate 10 --time-limit 20

The runs are independent, each with its own timing and faults. The attempt passes only if it builds and every run is valid.
I'll start by setting up the Go module and writing the node program.

Done. Implementation in `/work`:

- **`main.go`** — a single-node broadcast program built on `maelstrom.NewNode()`:
  - `broadcast`: records the integer message in a mutex-protected set, replies `broadcast_ok`.
  - `read`: replies `read_ok` with all recorded values (initialized non-nil, so it serializes as `[]` when empty).
  - `topology`: replies `topology_ok` (ignoring the graph, unused for one node).
  - `n.Run()` handles framing, the `init` reply, and the message loop.
- **`go.mod` / `go.sum`** — module `node` depending on the pre-cached Maelstrom Go library.

`go build -o node .` succeeds, and three separate runs of `maelstrom test --workload broadcast --bin ./node --node-count 1 --rate 10 --time-limit 20` all reported `:valid? true` with "Everything looks good!".
